title: Computational intelligence
summary:
Computational intelligence (CI) refers to concepts, paradigms, algorithms and implementations of systems designed to show intelligent behavior in complex and changing environments. These systems are aimed at mastering complex tasks and offer solutions that recognize and interpret patterns, control processes, support decision-making, or autonomously manoeuvre vehicles or robots in unknown environments.

These concepts and paradigms are characterized by the ability to learn or adapt to new situations, to generalize, to abstract, to discover and associate. Nature-analog or nature-inspired methods play a key role. The IEEE Computational Intelligence Society describes CI as the theory, design, application and development of biologically and linguistically motivated computational paradigms. Traditionally the three main pillars of CI have been Neural Networks, Fuzzy Systems, and Evolutionary Computation.

CI is an evolving field and also encompasses computing paradigms like ambient intelligence, artificial life, cultural learning, artificial endocrine networks, social reasoning, and artificial hormone networks. Evolutionary computation can be seen as a family of methods for global optimization based on a population of candidate solutions inspired by biological evolution, including genetic algorithms, evolution strategy, and genetic programming.

The distinction between CI and traditional AI goes back to Zadeh, the founder of fuzzy set theory, who differentiated machine intelligence into hard and soft computing techniques. In traditional AI, inaccuracy and uncertainty are undesirable, while CI focuses on dealing with these characteristics. Another distinguishing feature is the representation of information in symbolic form in AI versus sub-symbolic form in CI techniques. Deep learning has become the core method for AI, and some of the most successful AI systems are based on CI.
